Keywords: padding and changing a wound covering
RagShortTexts: Injured people need coverings, transport and continued care, with damp and dirt affecting comfort.
Woodland moss absorbs water but carries debris and cannot guarantee a sound wound.

Variants.Content:
After an injury in woodland, available padding, wrapping and carrying materials help move someone off cold wet ground. Cloth, clothing and timber can be borrowed; absorbent moss also carries mud, leaves and insects and needs replacing when wet. Covering a wound, limiting bleeding and sheltering a person are distinct needs that one material may not meet.

At shelter the injured still need food, drink, cleaning and observation. Pain, fever or inability to eat brings further appeals for help. A temporary covering is not the end: carers lose sleep and relatives take over work and fuel gathering. If a party moves on, carrying the patient or leaving a companion depends on carts and food as well as willingness.
Stewards tracking one issue of coverings miss continuing care and transport. Beds and family food belong alongside remedy costs.
A fallen companion needs carriers, redistributed loads and help at the destination. One wrapping does not restore ordinary marching ability on wet, cold ground.
Washable cloth is limited and loans or washing create obligations. Long care needs food, fuel and relief, with a neighbour’s night watch easing exhaustion.
